The Past Perfect and the Simple Past Tenses
In a narrative (spoken or written) when you want to refer to different past events, you can use either the Simple Past or the Past Perfect.
You use the Past Perfect to be precise about which event happened before another event. This is especially useful when you have many past actions being described in an non-sequential order.

Once you have introduced the scenario to your readers or listeners, and they understand that you are talking about events before another past event, you can use the Simple Past to continue the story. You don't have to continue using the Past Perfect.

For example:
We bought a new computer last month. Up until then, we had used my sister's but is started (had started) to act up and she needed (had needed) it back anyway. We took (had taken) it to the repair shop but that didn't solve (hadn't solved) the issues we were having.
If you use time markers to make the order of events clear, you can use either the Simple Past or the Past Perfect.

For example:
After Harold finished his work ... (or After Harold had finished his work ...)

Talk about something you did when you were a child.
Instructions: Complete the following steps. Fill in the Self Assessment.

images.text:
I fully realized that father was gone forever when I walked into his workshop. I think I had expected to walk in the door and find him hunched over his workbench. I had expected him to turn around and give me a knife so I could join him while he whittled away, making some small wooden animal or toy.
As I stood there looking at the empty workbench, I remembered the time I had spent with him in that room. My mother had died when I was eight years old. My father, seemingly anxious and hardworking man, only felt calm and relaxed when he was carving a piece of wood. This he did whenever he could.

As I got older, spending time with Dad in his workshop seemed boring. After I had started going to high school, my extra time had been taken up with other things. When I saw Dad in the workshop, I stopped and said hello, but rarely sat with him. Of course, when I went away to university we grew even further apart. I went home now and then for a holiday when I could, but that wasn't often.

By the time I had started working, our weekly talk had become monthly. The visits became infrequent. However, after I had become a parent myself our visits became more regular. I sat with my dad while we both whittled away at the wood. I talked about my life, often with my own son on my knee.
I discovered he was a sensitive, caring person with a deep insight into life and human nature. Over toy cars and little boats, I gained new respect for the man sitting next to me. All these memories had come flooding back to me as I stood staring at the empty workshop.
